column2:
SELECT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) rnk
  FROM emp)
WHERE rnk = :n;
Use DENSE_RANK so ties don't skip ranks. Add DISTINCT on outer if needed.

column1: PATTERN: Top N rows per group (exactly N, no ties)
column2:
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT e.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) rn
  FROM emp e)
WHERE rn <= 3;
Window functions can't go in WHERE, so filter in an outer query.

column1: PATTERN: Top 3 salaries per department INCLUDING ties
column2:
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) dr
  FROM emp e)
WHERE dr <= 3;

SELECT email, COUNT(*)
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

DELETE FROM users
WHERE ROWID NOT IN (
  SELECT MIN(ROWID) FROM users GROUP BY email);
ROWID is Oracle-only. Other DBs: use ROW_NUMBER() in a CTE, or self-join on id.

SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY cust_id ORDER BY order_date
                  ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
Specify ROWS explicitly; default is RANGE, which treats ties as peers.

AVG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day
                ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

column1: PATTERN: Compare to previous / next row
column2:
LAG(sal, 1, 0)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date)  -- previous
LEAD(sal, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date)  -- next
Args: (column, offset, default).

column1: PATTERN: Consecutive values / gaps and islands
column2:
SELECT MIN(id) start_id, MAX(id) end_id
FROM (SELECT id, id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) grp FROM t)
GROUP BY grp;
Consecutive ids give the same (id - row_number) constant. Group by it.

date_col - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY date_col) grp
In Oracle DATE minus number works directly. Group by grp, HAVING COUNT(*) >= N.

column1: PATTERN: Rows in A that never appear in B (anti-join)
column2:
-- Option 1
SELECT a.* FROM a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.a_id = a.id);
-- Option 2
SELECT a.* FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.a_id = a.id WHERE b.a_id IS NULL;
Avoid NOT IN if the subquery can return NULL: it returns zero rows.

SELECT dept_id,
  SUM(CASE WHEN job='CLERK'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) clerks,
  SUM(CASE WHEN job='MANAGER' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) managers
FROM emp GROUP BY dept_id;

SELECT * FROM (SELECT dept_id, job, sal FROM emp)
PIVOT (SUM(sal) FOR job IN ('CLERK' AS clerk, 'MANAGER' AS mgr));

SELECT * FROM sales
UNPIVOT (amount FOR quarter IN (q1 AS 'Q1', q2 AS 'Q2', q3 AS 'Q3', q4 AS 'Q4'));

SELECT MEDIAN(salary) FROM emp;
-- or
SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) FROM emp;

amount / SUM(amount) OVER ()                       -- of grand total
amount / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY dept)    -- of dept total
RATIO_TO_REPORT(amount) OVER ()                  -- Oracle shortcut

column1: PATTERN: Employees earning more than their manager
column2:
SELECT e.name
FROM emp e JOIN emp m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
Self join. Note: Oracle table aliases take NO 'AS' keyword.

column1: PATTERN: Employees earning above their department average
column2:
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT e.*, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) avg_sal FROM emp e)
WHERE salary > avg_sal;

column1: PATTERN: Second highest salary, NULL if none
column2:
SELECT (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp
        WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp)) AS second_high
FROM dual;
The outer SELECT from dual guarantees one row (NULL) even if nothing matches.

column1: PATTERN: Customers who bought ALL products (relational division)
column2:
SELECT cust_id FROM orders
GROUP BY cust_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products);

column1: PATTERN: First / last value per group using KEEP (Oracle)
column2:
SELECT dept_id,
  MAX(salary) KEEP (DENSE_RANK FIRST ORDER BY hire_date) sal_of_earliest_hire,
  MAX(salary) KEEP (DENSE_RANK LAST  ORDER BY hire_date) sal_of_latest_hire
FROM emp GROUP BY dept_id;

SELECT dept_id, LISTAGG(name, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY name) names
FROM emp GROUP BY dept_id;
Fails with ORA-01489 if the result exceeds 4000 bytes (12.2+: ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE).

SELECT mth, rev,
  rev - LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY mth) AS change,
  ROUND(100*(rev - LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY mth)) / LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY mth), 2) pct
FROM monthly_rev;
Guard divide by zero with NULLIF(LAG(...), 0).

column1: PATTERN: Odd / even rows or ids
column2: WHERE MOD(id, 2) = 1 (odd), MOD(id,2) = 0 (even). Oracle has MOD(), not the % operator.

SELECT CASE WHEN MOD(id,2)=1 AND id = (SELECT MAX(id) FROM seat) THEN id
            WHEN MOD(id,2)=1 THEN id + 1
            ELSE id - 1 END AS id, student
FROM seat ORDER BY id;
SELECT LEVEL n FROM dual CONNECT BY LEVEL <= 10;

column1: PATTERN: Generate a date series in Oracle
column2:
SELECT DATE '2026-01-01' + LEVEL - 1 AS d
FROM dual CONNECT BY LEVEL <= 31;

SELECT LEVEL, LPAD(' ', 2*(LEVEL-1)) || name AS name,
       SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(name, '/') path
FROM emp
START WITH manager_id IS NULL
CONNECT BY PRIOR emp_id = manager_id
ORDER SIBLINGS BY name;
PRIOR sits on the PARENT side. PRIOR emp_id = manager_id walks top-down. Also: CONNECT_BY_ROOT, CONNECT_BY_ISLEAF.

column1: PATTERN: Hierarchy with recursive CTE (works in Oracle 11gR2+)
column2:
WITH org (emp_id, name, manager_id, lvl) AS (
  SELECT emp_id, name, manager_id, 1 FROM emp WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.lvl + 1
  FROM emp e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.emp_id)
SELECT * FROM org;
Oracle: NO 'RECURSIVE' keyword, but column list is required. Postgres/MySQL: WITH RECURSIVE.

MERGE INTO target t
USING source s ON (t.id = s.id)
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.val = s.val
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (id, val) VALUES (s.id, s.val);

column1: PATTERN: Update one table from another (Oracle)
column2:
UPDATE t1
SET val = (SELECT s.val FROM t2 s WHERE s.id = t1.id)
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t2 s WHERE s.id = t1.id);
Oracle has no UPDATE ... JOIN. Use correlated subquery or MERGE. Without the EXISTS, unmatched rows get NULL.

column1: PATTERN: Users active on 2 consecutive days
column2:
SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         LAG(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) prev_d
  FROM logins)
WHERE login_date - prev_d = 1;

SELECT user_id, MIN(event_date) first_date
FROM events GROUP BY user_id;
-- then join back and compare event_date - first_date = 1

column1: PATTERN: Count rows including zero (group with no matches)
column2:
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id)
FROM dept d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_name;
COUNT(col) ignores NULLs, so use the right-side column. COUNT(*) would give 1 for empty groups.

column1: PATTERN: Filter on aggregate vs filter on row
column2: WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping. HAVING filters groups AFTER aggregation. Put non-aggregate conditions in WHERE for speed.

-- 12c+
SELECT * FROM emp ORDER BY sal DESC FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;
-- Older
SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM emp ORDER BY sal DESC) WHERE ROWNUM <= 5;
ROWNUM is assigned BEFORE ORDER BY. So WHERE ROWNUM <= 5 ORDER BY sal DESC does not give top 5. Sort in a subquery first. Also ROWNUM = 2 or ROWNUM > 1 return nothing.

SELECT * FROM emp ORDER BY id
OFFSET 10 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY;
In Oracle, '' (empty string) IS NULL. So WHERE col = '' never matches. Use IS NULL. This differs from Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server.
Table aliases: NO 'AS' (FROM emp e). Column aliases may use AS. Writing FROM emp AS e gives ORA-00933.

column1: ORACLE: Subquery in FROM needs an alias?
column2: No. Oracle allows FROM (SELECT ...) without an alias. MySQL, Postgres, SQL Server REQUIRE one. Add one anyway to be portable.

column1: ORACLE: Can I use a SELECT alias in WHERE / GROUP BY / HAVING?
column2: No. Aliases work only in ORDER BY. Repeat the expression, or wrap in a subquery/CTE. (Execution order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY.)
SELECT SYSDATE FROM dual; Oracle requires FROM. (Oracle 23c now allows SELECT without FROM.)
ROWID = physical address of the row (permanent, fastest access, used for dedupe). ROWNUM = temporary sequence number assigned to result rows as they are fetched.
UNION (distinct), UNION ALL (keeps dups, faster), INTERSECT, MINUS (Oracle's EXCEPT). Both queries need same column count and compatible types.

NVL(a, b)            -- a if not null else b
NVL2(a, x, y)        -- x if a not null else y
NULLIF(a, b)         -- NULL if a = b else a
COALESCE(a, b, c)    -- first non-null (ANSI, portable)
DECODE(a, 1,'one', 2,'two', 'other')  -- Oracle's CASE (NULL = NULL is true in DECODE)

col = NULL            -> never true. Use IS NULL.
NOT IN (list w/ NULL) -> returns no rows. Use NOT EXISTS.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs.
SUM/AVG ignore NULLs. AVG of (10, NULL, 20) = 15.
NULL || 'abc' = 'abc' in Oracle (NULL treated as empty in concat).
ORDER BY: NULLs sort LAST in ASC in Oracle (use NULLS FIRST/LAST).

SYSDATE                       -- current date + time (DB server)
TRUNC(SYSDATE)                -- strip time -> midnight
SYSDATE + 7                   -- add 7 days
d1 - d2                       -- difference in DAYS (number, may be fractional)
ADD_MONTHS(d, 3)
MONTHS_BETWEEN(d1, d2)
LAST_DAY(d)
TRUNC(d, 'MM')                -- first day of month
TRUNC(d, 'YYYY')              -- first day of year
NEXT_DAY(d, 'MONDAY')
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)

DATE '2026-01-31'
TO_DATE('31-01-2026', 'DD-MM-YYYY')
TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')
TO_CHAR(d, 'DY')     -- MON    'Day' -> Monday    'MON' -> JAN
TO_CHAR(d, 'Q')      -- quarter

column1: ORACLE: Compare a DATE column to a day (time part trap)
column2:
WHERE order_dt >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND order_dt <  DATE '2026-01-02'
Avoid TRUNC(order_dt) = ... on indexed columns (kills the index). Use a half-open range.

SUBSTR(s, start, len)         -- start can be negative (from end)
INSTR(s, sub [, start, nth])  -- position, 0 if not found
LENGTH(s)  UPPER(s)  LOWER(s)  INITCAP(s)
TRIM(s)  LTRIM(s)  RTRIM(s)
LPAD(s, 5, '0')  RPAD(s, 5, '*')
REPLACE(s, 'a', 'b')
TRANSLATE(s, 'abc', 'xyz')    -- char-by-char mapping
s1 || s2                      -- concat (CONCAT takes only 2 args)

REGEXP_LIKE(col, '^[A-Z]{3}[0-9]+$')
REGEXP_SUBSTR(col, '[0-9]+', 1, 1)
REGEXP_REPLACE(col, '[^0-9]', '')
REGEXP_INSTR(col, '@')
REGEXP_COUNT(col, ',')

SELECT REGEXP_SUBSTR('a,b,c', '[^,]+', 1, LEVEL) val
FROM dual
CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT('a,b,c', ',') + 1;
Oracle string comparison is CASE-SENSITIVE: 'abc' <> 'ABC'. Use UPPER(col) = 'ABC' (MySQL is case-insensitive by default).

CREATE TABLE emp_copy AS SELECT * FROM emp;
CREATE TABLE emp_empty AS SELECT * FROM emp WHERE 1 = 0;   -- structure only

-- 12c+
id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
-- classic
CREATE SEQUENCE emp_seq START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 1;
INSERT INTO emp (id) VALUES (emp_seq.NEXTVAL);
emp_seq.CURRVAL
With ORDER BY and no frame, default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. So LAST_VALUE returns the CURRENT row. Fix: add ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
Oracle NUMBER division is decimal: 5/2 = 2.5. In SQL Server / older Postgres integer / integer = 2. Use TRUNC(5/2) or FLOOR for integer result in Oracle.
WHERE a.id = b.id(+)   -- LEFT JOIN a to b  (+ goes on the optional side)

SELECT /*+ INDEX(e emp_dept_ix) */ * FROM emp e WHERE dept_id = 10;
/*+ FULL(e) */   /*+ PARALLEL(e, 4) */   /*+ LEADING(a b) USE_NL(b) */

EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT * FROM emp WHERE dept_id = 10;
SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY);

column1: DELTA: Top N rows  (Oracle | MySQL | Postgres | SQL Server)
column2:
Oracle: FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY / ROWNUM<=n
MySQL: LIMIT n
Postgres: LIMIT n
SQL Server: SELECT TOP n

Oracle: SYSDATE / SYSTIMESTAMP
MySQL: NOW() / CURDATE()
Postgres: NOW() / CURRENT_DATE
SQL Server: GETDATE()

Oracle: d1 - d2
MySQL: DATEDIFF(d1, d2)
Postgres: d1 - d2 (DATE) or EXTRACT(DAY FROM ...)
SQL Server: DATEDIFF(day, d2, d1) (note arg order!)

Oracle: d + n, ADD_MONTHS(d, n)
MySQL: DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL n DAY)
Postgres: d + INTERVAL '1 day'
SQL Server: DATEADD(day, n, d)

Oracle: NVL / COALESCE
MySQL: IFNULL / COALESCE
Postgres: COALESCE
SQL Server: ISNULL / COALESCE
COALESCE works everywhere.

Oracle: ||
MySQL: CONCAT()
Postgres: ||
SQL Server: + or CONCAT()

Oracle: SUBSTR
MySQL: SUBSTRING / SUBSTR
Postgres: SUBSTRING / SUBSTR
SQL Server: SUBSTRING (3 args required)

Oracle: MINUS
Postgres / SQL Server: EXCEPT
MySQL: NOT EXISTS (EXCEPT only in 8.0.31+)

Oracle: TO_CHAR(d,'YYYY-MM-DD')
MySQL: DATE_FORMAT(d,'%Y-%m-%d')
Postgres: TO_CHAR(d,'YYYY-MM-DD')
SQL Server: FORMAT(d,'yyyy-MM-dd') / CONVERT

Oracle: LISTAGG(x, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x)
MySQL: GROUP_CONCAT(x SEPARATOR ',')
Postgres / SQL Server: STRING_AGG(x, ',')

column1: DELTA: Dummy table for SELECT without a table
column2:
Oracle: FROM dual (23c optional)
MySQL / Postgres / SQL Server: not needed

Oracle: IDENTITY (12c+) or SEQUENCE
MySQL: AUTO_INCREMENT
Postgres: SERIAL / IDENTITY
SQL Server: IDENTITY(1,1)

Oracle: MERGE or correlated subquery
MySQL: UPDATE t1 JOIN t2 ON ... SET ...
Postgres: UPDATE t1 SET ... FROM t2 WHERE ...
SQL Server: UPDATE t1 SET ... FROM t1 JOIN t2 ...

Oracle: WITH name (cols) AS (...) no RECURSIVE
SQL Server: WITH name AS (...) no RECURSIVE
Postgres / MySQL 8: WITH RECURSIVE
Oracle also has CONNECT BY.

Oracle: MEDIAN(x) or PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x)
Postgres: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (...)
MySQL: no built-in, use window function trick
SQL Server: PERCENTILE_CONT(...) OVER ()
Oracle and SQL Server have PIVOT keyword. MySQL and Postgres: use SUM(CASE WHEN ...) (Postgres also has crosstab in tablefunc).

Oracle / Postgres: "double quotes" (case-sensitive when quoted)
MySQL: `backticks`
SQL Server: [brackets]
String literals: single quotes everywhere.

Oracle: '' = NULL
All the others: '' is an empty, non-NULL string.

FROM / JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT (incl. window functions) -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> FETCH/LIMIT.
Why aliases work in ORDER BY only, and window functions can't be in WHERE.
WHERE filters rows before grouping (no aggregates). HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

column1: THEORY: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK
column2:
Scores 100, 90, 90, 80:
ROW_NUMBER: 1,2,3,4
RANK: 1,2,2,4 (gap)
DENSE_RANK: 1,2,2,3 (no gap)
UNION removes duplicates (sort/distinct step, slower). UNION ALL keeps all rows (faster). Default to UNION ALL when duplicates are impossible or acceptable.
INNER: matches only. LEFT: all left + matches. RIGHT: all right + matches. FULL OUTER: all from both. CROSS: cartesian product. SELF: table joined to itself. Semi-join: EXISTS. Anti-join: NOT EXISTS.

EXISTS stops at first match, handles NULLs safely, good when the outer set is small and inner is indexed. IN suits a small, static list. NOT IN breaks if the list contains NULL. Modern optimizers often rewrite them the same.

column1: THEORY: Subquery vs CTE vs temp table vs view
column2: Subquery: inline, one use. CTE (WITH): named, readable, reusable within a single statement. Global temporary table (Oracle): stores rows for session/transaction, indexable. View: stored query, no data. Materialized view: stored query WITH data, refreshed.
Non-correlated runs once independently. Correlated references the outer row, so it conceptually runs per outer row (often rewritten as a join/window).
B-tree (default, high cardinality). Bitmap (low cardinality, DW, bad for heavy DML). Function-based (index on UPPER(col)). Composite (column order matters: leftmost prefix). Unique. Reverse-key.

A condition that can use an index. NOT sargable: WHERE TRUNC(dt) = ..., WHERE UPPER(name) = 'X' (without function index), WHERE col + 1 = 5, LIKE '%abc'. Sargable: WHERE dt >= ... AND dt < ..., LIKE 'abc%'.

column1: THEORY: Clustered vs non-clustered index (and Oracle's equivalent)
column2: Clustered: table rows physically ordered by key (one per table). Non-clustered: separate structure with pointers. Oracle's equivalent of a clustered index is an Index-Organized Table (IOT); normal tables are heaps.

column1: THEORY: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
column2: DELETE: DML, row by row, WHERE allowed, rollback-able, fires triggers. TRUNCATE: DDL, removes all rows fast, auto-commits, resets high-water mark, no WHERE. DROP: removes the table itself.

Atomicity (all or nothing). Consistency (valid state to valid state). Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere). Durability (committed data survives crashes). Oracle default isolation: READ COMMITTED.

1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependency (non-key depends only on the key). BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key.
PRIMARY KEY (unique + not null, one per table). UNIQUE (allows NULL). FOREIGN KEY (referential integrity). NOT NULL. CHECK. DEFAULT.
COMMIT makes changes permanent. ROLLBACK undoes uncommitted changes. SAVEPOINT name; ROLLBACK TO name; undoes part. DDL (CREATE, TRUNCATE, ALTER) in Oracle auto-commits.
Range (dates), List (regions), Hash (even spread), Composite. Benefits: partition pruning, easier archiving (drop/exchange partition), parallelism.
Stored query result. Refresh: COMPLETE / FAST (needs MV logs) / FORCE. ON DEMAND or ON COMMIT. Can enable query rewrite.

1) Read EXPLAIN PLAN (full scans, cardinality). 2) Add/adjust indexes. 3) Avoid functions on indexed columns. 4) Select only needed columns. 5) Filter early. 6) Prefer EXISTS / joins over big IN lists. 7) Gather stats (DBMS_STATS). 8) Use bind variables.
Placeholders (:id) so Oracle reuses one parsed plan instead of hard parsing each literal. Improves performance and prevents SQL injection.

column1: THEORY: Stored procedure vs function vs trigger (PL/SQL)
column2: Procedure: performs actions, may return via OUT params, not usable in SELECT. Function: must RETURN a value, usable in SQL. Trigger: fires automatically on DML/DDL events. Package: groups related procs/functions.

DECLARE
  v_sal NUMBER;
BEGIN
  SELECT salary INTO v_sal FROM emp WHERE emp_id = 1;
EXCEPTION
  WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN NULL;
  WHEN TOO_MANY_ROWS THEN NULL;
END;
Implicit: Oracle creates automatically for each DML / SELECT INTO (attributes SQL%ROWCOUNT, SQL%FOUND). Explicit: declared, OPEN / FETCH / CLOSE, or FOR rec IN cur LOOP.

column1: STRATEGY: First 30 seconds of any SQL question
column2: 1) Restate the problem. 2) Ask about NULLs, ties, duplicates, empty results. 3) Say: 'I'll use Oracle syntax; I know the MySQL/Postgres equivalents.' 4) Name the pattern aloud (e.g., top-N per group -> ROW_NUMBER).

column1: STRATEGY: If I blank on syntax
column2: Say what the function should do, write a close version, and note 'exact syntax may vary by DB'. Interviewers grade logic over punctuation. Then fix it once you recall.

column1: STRATEGY: Build the query in layers
column2: 1) FROM + JOIN. 2) WHERE. 3) GROUP BY + aggregates. 4) Window function. 5) Wrap in subquery/CTE and filter on the window result. 6) ORDER BY. Check each layer mentally with 3 sample rows.

'Nth / top N' -> DENSE_RANK / ROW_NUMBER. 'Consecutive' -> gaps and islands or LAG. 'Never / no' -> NOT EXISTS. 'Running / cumulative' -> SUM OVER. 'Compared to previous' -> LAG. 'Each X has at least' -> GROUP BY + HAVING. 'Hierarchy / manager chain' -> CONNECT BY / recursive CTE.
